UNITED STATES OF AMERICA
DEPARTMENT OF THE TREASURY
FINANCIAL CRIMES ENFORCEMENT NETWORK
IN THE MATTER OF No. 2001 - 02
ANGELINA PLETT
ASSESSMENT OF CIVIL MONEY PENALTIES
AGAINST ANGELINA PLETT
I. INTRODUCTION
The Secretary of the United States Department of the Treasury has delegated to
the Director of the Financial Crimes Enforcement Network (“FinCEN”) the authority to
determine whether a financial institution has violated the Bank Secrecy Act, 31 U.S.C.
§§5311 et seq. and 31 CFR Part 103 thereunder (“BSA”), and what, if any, sanction is
appropriate.
II. JURISDICTION
Angelina Plett (“Plett”) was, at all relevant times, an owner and the manager of
Cash For Checks Inc. (“Cash For Checks”). Cash For Checks was, at all relevant times, a
licensed check casher located in Oklahoma City, Oklahoma and was a “financial
institution” within the meaning of 31 U.S.C. §5312(a)(2) and 31 CFR §103.11(n).1
III. FINCEN’S DETERMINATIONS
A. Structuring
FinCEN has determined that between July 11, 1995, and April 26, 1996, Plett
willfully structured or willfully assisted in structuring check cashing transactions for
Joseph A. Sivigliano (“Sivigliano”) through a domestic financial institution in violation
of 31 U.S.C. §5324(a)(3) and 31 CFR §103.63(c). During the relevant time period,
Sivigliano cashed 136 checks totaling more than $1.17 million at Cash For Checks. On
each of 43 days, Sivigliano cashed a series of checks that individually totaled less than
$10,000, but that together exceeded $10,0

Conclusions of La/iv A person is required to file a currency transaction report when said person or his agent, “knowingly transports, is *1228 about to transport, or has transported, monetary instruments of more than $10,000 at one time from a place in the United States to or through a place outside the United States.” 31 U.S.C. § 5316 (a)(1)(A). This reporting requirement applies to [e]ach person who physically transports ... or causes to be physically transported ... currency or other monetary instruments in an aggregate amount exceeding $10,000 at one time from the United States to any place outside the United States .... A person is deemed to have caused such transportation ... when he aids, abets, counsels, commands, procures, or requests it to be done by a financial institution or another person. 31 C.F.R. § 103.23 (2005). In fleshing out what it means for a person to transport currency “at one time,” 31 C.F.R. § 103.11 (2005) sets forth the following criteria: (1) That person either alone, in conjunction with or on behalf of others; (2) Transports, mails, ships or receives in any manner; is about to transport, mail or ship in any manner; or causes the transportation, mailing, shipment or receipt in any manner of; (3) Monetary instruments; (4) Into the United States or out of the United States; (5) Totaling more than $10,000; (6) (i) On one calendar day or (ii) if for the purpose of evading the reporting requirements of section 103.23

statutory.question: Does the conduct described fall within 5324?
statutory.answer: Yes, 31 U.S.C. § 5324 prohibits structuring transactions to evade reporting requirements, and the pattern of deposits suggests such intent.
statutory.label: entailment
statutory.reasoning: Under 31 U.S.C. § 5324, it is unlawful to structure transactions to evade the reporting requirements of a Currency Transaction Report (CTR), which is triggered by cash deposits exceeding $10,000. The fact pattern shows Entity SYN_3fd1007f conducted 12 cash deposits between 2026-04-12 and 2026-04-21, all of which were kept below the $10,000 threshold (ranging from $5,270.80 to $9,676.64). Notably, these deposits occurred across multiple different branches (DFW, ATL, LAX, MIA, ORD, Port Authority, Greyhound Terminal) in a very short timeframe. This behavior of splitting large sums into smaller amounts across various locations is a classic indicator that 31 U.S.C. § 5324 prohibits structuring to avoid the filing of a CTR.

Each transaction was kept below the $10,000 reporting threshold, ranging from $5,270.80 to $9,676.64. Notably, these deposits were dispersed across multiple disparate branches, including DFW, ATL, LAX, MIA, ORD, Port Authority, and Greyhound Terminal, which is inconsistent with the normal operations of a single convenience store. Behavioral metrics indicate a volume ratio of 2.9x relative to the declared monthly volume of $102,652.0. This activity appears designed to evade Currency Transaction Report (CTR) requirements in violation of 31 U.S.C. § 5324. We defer the final filing decision to the human investigator.
